{{more footnotes|date=February 2023}}

{{Short description|Integrable classical system}}

In [[mathematical physics]], the '''Garnier integrable system''', also known as the '''classical Gaudin model''', is a [[classical mechanics|classical mechanical system]] discovered by René Garnier<ref name="Garnier">{{cite journal |last1=Garnier |first1= René |title=Sur une classe de systèmes différentiels abéliens déduits de la théorie des équations linéaires |journal=Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo |date=December 1919 |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=155–191 |doi=10.1007/BF03014668|s2cid=120557738 }}</ref> in 1917, and solved using abelian integrals on compact Riemann surfaces (algebraic curves) of arbitrarily high genus.  It is obtained by taking the '[[Paul Painlevé|Painlevé]] simplification' or 'autonomous limit' of the [[Schlesinger equations#Schlesinger's equations|Schlesinger equations]]<ref name="Chud">{{cite journal |last1=Chudnovsky |first1=D. V. |title=Simplified Schlesinger's systems |journal=Lettere al Nuovo Cimento |date=December 1979 |volume=26 |issue=14 |pages=423–427 |doi=10.1007/BF02817023|s2cid=122196561 }}</ref>. 
It may be interpreted as the classical limit of the [[Gaudin model|quantum Gaudin model]] due to [[Michel Gaudin (physicist)|Michel Gaudin]]<ref name="Gaudin">{{cite journal |last1=Gaudin |first1=Michel |title=Diagonalisation d'une classe d'hamiltoniens de spin |journal=Journal de Physique |date=1976 |volume=37 |issue=10 |pages=1087–1098 |doi=10.1051/jphys:0197600370100108700 |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/jpa-00208506/document |access-date=26 September 2022}}</ref>. 
(Similarly, the [[Schlesinger equations]] are the classical limit of the [[Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations]], expressed in the Heisenberg representation.<ref name="Resh">{{cite journal |last1=Reshetikhin |first1=N. |title=The Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov system as a deformation of the isomonodromy problem |journal=Lett. Math. Phys. |date=1992 |volume=26 |pages=166-177 |doi=10.1007/BF00420750 }}</ref><ref name = "Har1">{{cite journal |last1=Harnad |first1=J. |title=Quantum Isomonodromic Deformations and the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov Equations |journal=CRM Proceedings and Lecture Note Series 9, (eds. D. Levi, L. Vinet and P. Winternitz)  |date=1996 |volume=9 |pages=155-161  }} </ref>. )

The Garnier systems were later shown to be of Hamiltonian type <ref name= "AHP">{{cite journal | last1=Adams | first1=M.  | last2=Harnad | first2=J. | last3= Previato | first3= E. | title=Isospectral Hamiltonian Flows in Finite and Infinite  Dimensions. I. Generalized Moser Problem and Moment Maps into Loop Algebras | journal=Commun.  Math. Phys.  | date=1988 | volume=117 |pages=451-500  }} </ref>
<ref name = "AHH1">{{cite journal | last1=Adams | first1=M.  | last2=Harnad | first2=J. | last3= Hurtubise | first3= J. | title=Isospectral Hamiltonian Flows in Finite and Infinite Dimensions II. Integration of Flows | journal =Commun.  Math. Phys.   | date=1990 | volume=134 |pages=555-585 }} </ref>
<ref name ="AHH2">{{cite journal | last1=Adams | first1=M.  | last2=Harnad | first2=J. | last3= Hurtubise | first3=J. | title=Darboux Coordinates and Liouville-Arnold  integration in Loop Algebras | journal =Commun. Math. Phys. | date =1993 |volume=155 | pages =385-413  }} </ref>, defined on a phase space consisting of the [[Cartesian product]] of <math>N</math> copies of the dual <math>\mathfrak{gl(r)}^*</math> of the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{gl(r)}^*</math>, for <math>N</math> a positive integer, and  [[integrable system|completely integrable]] in the Hamiltonian sense.

They are also a specific case of [[Hitchin system|Hitchin integrable system]]s, when the [[algebraic curve]] that the theory is defined on is the [[Riemann sphere]] and the system is [[tamely ramified]].

== As a limit of the Schlesinger equations ==
The [[Schlesinger equations]] are a system of differential equations for <math>n + 2</math> matrix-valued functions <math>A_i:\mathbb{C}^{n+2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mat}(m, \mathbb{C})</math>, given by
<math display = block> \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial \lambda_j} = \frac{[A_i,A_j]}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j} \qquad \qquad j\neq i </math>
<math display = block>\sum_j \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial \lambda_j} = 0.</math>

The 'autonomous limit' is given by replacing the <math>\lambda_i</math> dependence in the denominator by constants <math>\alpha_i</math> with <math>\alpha_{n+1} = 0, \alpha_{n+2} = 1</math>:
<math display = block> \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial \lambda_j} = \frac{[A_i,A_j]}{\alpha_i-\alpha_j} \qquad \qquad j\neq i </math>
<math display = block> \sum_j \frac{\partial A_i}{\partial \lambda_j} = 0.</math>
This is the '''Garnier system''' in the form originally derived by Garnier.

== As the classical Gaudin model ==
There is a formulation of the Garnier system as a classical mechanical system, the classical Gaudin model, which quantizes to the quantum Gaudin model and whose equations of motion are equivalent to the Garnier system. This section describes this formulation.<ref name="AHP" /><ref name="AHH1" /><ref name="AHH2" /><ref>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |last=Lacroix |first=Sylvain |date=2018 |title= Modéles intégrables avec fonction twist et modèles de Gaudin affines|publisher=[[University of Lyon]]}}</ref>

As for any classical system, the Gaudin model is specified by a [[Poisson manifold]] <math>M</math> referred to as the [[phase space]], and a [[smooth function]] on the manifold called the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]].

=== Phase space ===
Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a quadratic [[Lie algebra]], that is, a Lie algebra with a non-[[degenerate form|degenerate]] [[invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] [[bilinear form]] <math>\kappa</math>. If <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is [[complex vector space|complex]] and [[simple Lie algebra|simple]], this can be taken to be the [[Killing form]].

The [[dual vector space|dual]], denoted <math>\mathfrak{g}^*</math>, can be made into a [[Poisson manifold#linear Poisson structure|linear Poisson structure]] by the [[coadjoint orbit|Kirillov–Kostant bracket]].

The phase space <math>M</math> of the classical Gaudin model is then the [[Cartesian product]] of <math>N</math> copies of <math>\mathfrak{g}^*</math> for <math>N</math> a positive integer.

=== Sites ===
Associated to each of these copies is a point in <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, denoted <math>\lambda_1, \cdots, \lambda_N</math>, and referred to as '''sites'''.

=== Lax matrix ===
Fixing a basis of the Lie algebra <math>\{I^a\}</math> with [[structure constant]]s <math>f^{ab}_c</math>, there are functions <math>X^a_{(r)}</math> with <math>r = 1, \cdots, N</math> on the phase space satisfying the Poisson bracket
<math display = block>\{X^a_{(r)}, X^b_{(s)}\} = \delta_{rs}f^{ab}_c X^c_{(r)}.</math>

These in turn are used to define <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-valued functions
<math display = block>X^{(r)} = \kappa_{ab}I^a \otimes X^b_{(r)}</math>
with [[Einstein summation convention|implicit summation]].

Next, these are used to define the [[Lax pair|Lax matrix]] which is also a <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> valued function on the phase space which in addition depends [[meromorphic]]ally on a spectral parameter <math>\lambda</math>,
<math display = block>\mathcal{L}(\lambda) = \sum_{r = 1}^N \frac{X^{(r)}}{\lambda - \lambda_r} + \Omega,</math>
and <math>\Omega</math> is a constant element in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, in the sense that it Poisson commutes (has vanishing Poisson bracket) with all functions.

=== (Quadratic) Hamiltonian ===
The (quadratic) Hamiltonian is
<math display = block>\mathcal{H}(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2}\kappa(\mathcal{L}(\lambda), \mathcal{L}(\lambda))</math>
which is indeed a function on the phase space, which is additionally dependent on a spectral parameter <math>\lambda</math>. This can be written as
<math display = block>\mathcal{H}(\lambda) = \Delta_\infty + \sum_{r = 1}^N\left( \frac{\Delta_r}{(\lambda - \lambda_r)^2} + 
\frac{\mathcal{H}_r}{\lambda - \lambda_r} \right),</math>
with 
<math display = block> \Delta_r = \frac{1}{2} \kappa(X^{(r)}, X^{(r)}), \Delta_\infty = \frac{1}{2} \kappa(\Omega, \Omega)</math>
and
<math display = block> \mathcal{H}_r = \sum_{s \neq r} \frac{ \kappa( X^{(r)}, X^{(s)} )}{ 
\lambda_r - \lambda_s} + \kappa(X^{(r)} , \Omega).</math>

From the Poisson bracket relation
<math display = block> \{ \mathcal{H}(\lambda), \mathcal{H}(\mu) \} = 0,  \forall \lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{C},</math>
by varying <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\mu</math> it must be true that the <math>\mathcal{H}_r</math>'s, the <math>\Delta_r</math>'s and <math>\Delta_\infty</math> are all in involution. It can be shown that the <math>\Delta_r</math>'s and <math>\Delta_\infty</math> Poisson commute with all functions on the phase space, but the <math>\mathcal{H}_r</math>'s do not in general. These are the conserved charges in involution for the purposes of [[Arnol'd–Liouville theorem|Arnol'd Liouville integrability]].

=== Lax equation ===
One can show
<math display = block> \{\mathcal{H}_r, \mathcal{L}(\lambda)\} = \left[\frac{X^{(r)}}{\lambda - \lambda_r}, \mathcal{L}(\lambda)\right], </math>
so the Lax matrix satisfies the Lax equation when time evolution is given by any of the Hamiltonians <math>\mathcal{H}_r</math>, as well as any linear combination of them.

=== Higher Hamiltonians ===
The quadratic Casimir gives corresponds to a quadratic [[Weyl group|Weyl invariant]] polynomial for the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, but in fact many more commuting conserved charges can be generated using <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-invariant polynomials. These invariant polynomials can be found using the [[Harish-Chandra isomorphism]] in the case <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is complex, simple and finite.

== Integrable field theories as classical Gaudin models ==
Certain integrable classical field theories can be formulated as classical affine Gaudin models, where <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is an [[affine Lie algebra]]. Such classical field theories include the principal [[chiral model]], coset [[sigma model]]s and affine [[Toda field theory]].<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Vicedo |first1=Benoit |title=On integrable field theories as dihedral affine Gaudin models |date=2017 |class=hep-th |eprint=1701.04856}}</ref> As such, affine Gaudin models can be seen as a 'master theory' for integrable systems, but is most naturally formulated in the Hamiltonian formalism, unlike other master theories like [[four-dimensional Chern–Simons theory]] or [[Yang–Mills equations|anti-self-dual Yang–Mills]].

== Quantum Gaudin models ==
{{Main article|Gaudin model}}
A great deal is known about the integrable structure of [[Gaudin model|quantum Gaudin model]]s. In particular, [[Boris Feigin|Feigin]], [[Edward Frenkel|Frenkel]] and [[Nicolai Reshetikhin|Reshetikhin]] studied them using the theory of [[vertex operator algebra]]s, showing the relation of Gaudin models to topics in mathematics including the [[Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equation]]s and the [[geometric Langlands correspondence]].<ref name="ffr">{{cite journal |last1=Feigin |first1=Boris |last2=Frenkel |first2=Edward |last3=Reshetikhin |first3=Nikolai |title=Gaudin Model, Bethe Ansatz and Critical Level |journal=Commun. Math. Phys. |date=3 Apr 1994 |volume=166 |issue=1 |pages=27–62 |doi=10.1007/BF02099300 |arxiv=hep-th/9402022 |bibcode=1994CMaPh.166...27F |s2cid=17099900 }}</ref>
